2025 was the year everyone bet on hyper-personalization. Many touchpoints per prospect. As much information about each recipient as the tools could gather.
Our 2026 outreach data pushed against that bet. Comparing AI-hyperpersonalized campaigns against the same accounts' human-written campaigns, human copy won on acceptance by 12%, and the reply rate stayed flat. The apparent lift in cross-account comparisons is selection bias: the operators using AI were already outperforming the platform average with their own templates.

What I think is happening:
Past a certain density of gathered detail, a message reads as surveillance rather than attention. It gets creepy. You collected all of this about someone so you could send them an automated message, and they can tell.
The scarce input in outbound has stopped being contact data. It's the moment that matters the most.
Someone engages with a post about a system problem you solve, and you know exactly what they're dealing with. That's a reason to reach out.
A prospect who signed a one-year contract with a competitor last month is probably unreachable no matter how good your copy is; the windows are around renewal or when something breaks.
So if you run outreach for clients, the money is better spent watching for buying signals than digging up more detail on each contact. A tool that tells you when someone starts hiring, changes jobs, or posts about the problem you solve is worth more than another data enrichment layer.

My great-grandfather, grandfather, and father were all union men who built careers on a simple contract: "Give us a lifetime commitment, and we will take care of you." In their industries, technology changed and retraining was simply expected so workers stayed relevant. I’m not advocating for union shops, but it’s striking how today's corporate environment treats skilled talent as disposable widgets rather than valued long-term assets.

Look at the current cycle. A company announces mass layoffs to "streamline." Concurrently, their careers page lists hundreds of open requisitions. Hundreds of millions vanish into restructuring charges—severance, outplacement, legal fees—while TA teams burn the candle at both ends sourcing external hires with "future-proof" skills. Not only are recruiters struggling—the market is flooded with resumes claiming deep AI expertise candidates couldn't possibly possess—but companies eat the massive reputation hit that comes with persistent downsizing.

It looks like chaos, but it’s driven by flawed financial incentives. Wall Street forgives multi-million-dollar restructuring charges as "one-time paper events," applauding management for "decisive cost discipline." Just recently, the day after news broke that Oracle was conducting another downsizing, their stock popped. Meanwhile, formal upskilling programs are logged as ongoing OpEx, directly eroding quarterly operating margins.

Combine that accounting theater with corporate impatience—the delusion that you can buy plug-and-play talent faster than you can build it—and you get an endless burn-and-replace loop. In reality, companies spend six to nine months hunting candidate unicorns, fighting offer wars, and waiting another year for new hires to figure out how the organization actually operates.

I did a little research on the topic. Gallup and SHRM data show replacing a skilled employee costs 1.5x to 2x their annual salary. Retraining is a viable financial hedge. When AT&T shifted to software, they invested $1 billion to upskill 100,000 employees, filling over 50% of new technical management roles from within. IBM took a similar path in cloud and AI, reallocating tens of thousands of workers and saving an estimated $300 million in hiring costs while keeping invaluable domain knowledge inside the building.

I fear we have a lack of vision in corporate leadership that looks no further than next quarter's earnings. Signing a severance check takes zero imagination. What requires real effort is corporate wisdom, executive courage, and an HR organization with the vision to see that institutional knowledge walking out the door is worth investing in. Employees are human capital, not temporary entries on a balance sheet.

Have you seen organizations actually get the retraining model right?  Is this a viable strategy these days?

⚙️ One thing I’ve noticed with automation: automating the happy path is the easy part.

We can automate a deployment, infrastructure provisioning, certificate renewal, scaling, or even incident remediation. The workflow works perfectly when everything happens exactly as expected.

Production rarely behaves that way.

The interesting work starts with the other 20%: What happens when a deployment succeeds but health checks fail? What if Terraform partially applies? What if an API times out halfway through a workflow? What if an automated remediation runs twice? What if the rollback itself fails?

This has changed how I think about automation. I don't only ask “Can we automate this?” I also think about “How does this automation fail safely?”

For the workflows I work on, I like having validation before execution, clear failure handling, retries only where they are safe, proper logging, rollback or recovery paths, and human approval when the action has a larger production impact.

The same thinking is becoming even more important with AI agents and AIOps. Giving an agent the ability to perform an action is easy. Making sure it knows when to stop, escalate, or ask for approval is the real engineering work.

💡 Good automation saves manual effort. Reliable automation also knows what to do when things don't go according to plan.

That’s the difference between a script that works and automation you can actually trust in production.

For companies doing business in or with the state, here are some things to pay attention to:

- Frontier AI companies — The AI Subcabinet is developing legislative recommendations covering safety testing, independent audits, whistleblower protections, and 72-hour incident reporting. Those developing or using AI should expect a formal regulatory framework to emerge from the 2027 session.

- Housing & lending (my favorite topic 😉 ) — DHCD is moving to prohibit algorithmic tenant-screening tools that discriminate in DHCD-financed properties, and the state will push legislation barring shared pricing platforms that use non-public competitor data to set rents. This has come up before in the General Assembly, but there's good reason to believe this is the year something will pass.

- Employment & HR tech — MCCR, the Department of Labor, DBM, and DoIT are issuing guidance clarifying that existing civil rights and discrimination laws already apply to AI-driven hiring, screening, and management tools. Employers using AI in HR workflows should audit those systems against current anti-discrimination law.

- Consumer-facing AI & minors — Expect new rules on chatbots, addictive algorithmic design for under-16 users, and classroom AI tools. If your AI tools interact with the Maryland public, you should start engaging with the administration and lawmakers now to familiarize them with your process.

Governor Moore is moving ahead of federal guardrails, and this framework may set the stage for AI-related legislation for the 2027 session. Companies with Maryland operations, contracts, or users should start assessing exposure now rather than waiting for bill text.

AI labs are hiring their own referees. Independence now has to be demonstrated.

On September 18, Anthropic, the company behind Claude, announced a partnership with Accenture to assess the safety of its AI. The scope is serious: red-teaming, alignment assessments, testing safeguards. The money is serious too: at least $1 billion combined over five years, and Anthropic funds Accenture's work directly.
The evaluators will work inside Anthropic. They will follow how its models are built, test their weaknesses and speak directly with staff.
That alone does not make the assessment unreliable. Companies pay outside auditors to check their accounts. But trust depends on the rules.
And some important rules are still being worked out: what these evaluators can access, and how they will report their findings.
For me, three questions matter:
1. Who pays?
Can the evaluator publish an uncomfortable finding without putting its contract at risk?
2. What can they inspect?
Can they examine failed tests and challenge decisions, or only see what the company chooses to share?
3. What will the public see?
Will we get the findings, their limits and the problems that remain?

I run a small creative studio in Paris. We use these tools. Our clients ask what they can trust.
A public report gives us evidence to discuss. A partnership announcement gives us names.
Anthropic says more evaluators will be announced soon. I’ll be looking for what they can investigate and what they can tell us afterwards.
So, what would help you trust an AI audit most: knowing who pays, what gets tested, or what the findings reveal?

Your 2027 headcount plan gets decided in the next 6 weeks. Most of it is built on outdated job descriptions. 📋

Before you approve a single req, ask one question: which roles do you build, which do you buy, and which do you rent?

🔹 Build: reskill people you already have into AI-related work
🔹 Buy: hire full-time for capabilities that stay core for 3+ years
🔹 Rent: bring in contract specialists for skills that will look different in 12 months

The mistake we see most is approving every AI role as a permanent hire. Then the team spends 60+ days searching for a profile that has changed by the time they find it. Nearly half of firms now say they'll pay an 11–15% premium for AI skills (KPMG), so a slow, wrong permanent hire costs more than ever.

Three questions for your planning meeting:
→ Will this role look the same a year from now?
→ What does a 90-day vacancy cost this project?
→ Could a contract specialist deliver now while you define the permanent role?

Get the mix right in October, and Q1 starts with people in seats instead of reqs on a board.

The Ratepayer Protection Act tells states to consider requiring that data centers and other large computing loads above 100 megawatts pay the full incremental cost of any new generation, transmission or distribution built to serve them.

Three months to our summit date. Then the earthquake hit Caracas.
José, our founder and CEO, lost his apartment there. 
Suddenly we were coordinating rescue efforts in Venezuela while the programme was still being built, and every sensible reason to postpone was sitting on the table.
We did not move the date.
Things derailed anyway. For a long stretch it looked bleak. Ten days out, the room was nowhere near full and the case for calling it off was easy to make.
Nobody called it off. We kept working the same systems, every day, and registrations more than doubled in the final ten days.
On 17 September the first Venezuela Reawakening Summit ran at the Hyatt Regency Houston West, days after the G20 Energy Ministerial in Houston and a historic U.S. and Venezuela oil agreement. The room was full. More than a hundred people joined from other continents.
A team this small does not hold a date that size by working harder. We held it by automating everything that did not need a human:
→ Bilingual AI agents: a voice line, a website chatbot, and drafted replies to the summit inbox
→ Email campaigns, reminders, receipts and confirmations, all automated
→ Registration, CRM, badges, the event app and AI generated floor maps
→ White paper intake, filing and AI synthesis
→ A live stream for everyone joining from other continents
None of that is the interesting part. The interesting part is what it freed the humans to do.
While the systems handled confirmations and follow-ups at 2am, the team was coordinating relief, holding speakers through a crisis, and keeping a fragile thing alive long enough to happen.
The white paper is still being written. A sneak peek at what is coming out of it:
48 contributors submitted across four working sessions. We have read every one.
It is not really about money. It is about people, and about improving lives.
Almost nobody asked for capital. They asked for rules they can rely on. Licences long enough to finance against. Published contract models. Defined liability. Dispute resolution that does not depend on a local court. The money is there. What is missing is the certainty that lets someone hire, train and build.
Running underneath all of it: workforce, training, knowledge transfer, community trust, local hiring. The rules matter because of what they let people do.
Follow along to learn what businesses in the United States and Venezuela are asking for. The full white paper is coming shortly. The one-page recap is attached.
Human First. AI Assisted.

💷 This week, we'll be revealing the industry's 5 greatest financial challenges, to help staffing agencies prepare their response.

2️⃣ Second on the list is Fee Erosion:

💰 The Office for National Statistics reports that UK vacancies have fallen to their lowest levels since 2014 (outside of the pandemic). Dramatically shrinking vacancies means fierce competition, seeing many staffing firms resort to heavy discounts to win exclusive roles

💰 Whilst agency job postings are falling, direct employer job postings are stabilizing. Employers are increasingly using internal talent acquisition teams and AI automation to cut out recruitment intermediaries entirely. Growing self-serve capabilities mean that when employers do engage external agencies, they're in a better position to negotiate much lower fees

💰 Economic uncertainty is also encouraging employers to pivot away from executive search and expensive perm placements, towards more agile staffing options. Traditional high-inflation percentage fees based on high annual salaries are plummeting in popularity, compared with temporary and contract models

💰 Legislation including the Employment Rights Act have seen employers  absorb much higher wage bills. Hiring managers are limited to tighter budgets, and are seeking to drive down talent acquisition costs to protect their own cash flows.

55% of Deel’s Legal department is already automated with 3 AI agents.
Read that again before hiring your next 10 people.

Because the craziest part isn’t the 55%.

It’s how they built them.

- No army of AI engineers.
- No 6-month “AI transformation.”
- No “let’s give everyone a Claude account.”

Their lawyers showed Akai how they work.

It watched.

Then it built the workflows.
Take contract redlining.
~200 requests a week.

100+ countries.

- Different laws.
- Different clauses.
- Different edge cases.

Akai watches how lawyers handle them and learns the process.

But here’s the part that got me.

A lawyer interpreted a clause, then checked the actual statute before making the call.

Akai noticed those were two separate steps and created this rule: “Never clear a clause on interpretation alone.”

Nobody explicitly told it that. It learned it from the way the lawyer worked.

Then 3 lawyers overrode it on the same indemnity clause.

Akai spotted the pattern.

The playbook said one thing.
The lawyers were consistently doing another.

So it proposed changing the rule and attached the evidence behind the decision.

A lawyer still had to approve it.

Think about that.

Most companies are spending months trying to write perfect SOPs so AI can understand how they operate.

That may be backwards.

Your best employees already know how the company operates.

- Watch them.
- Capture the decisions.
- Turn that judgment into infrastructure.

Then let every correction make the system better.

That’s a much bigger idea than another “AI agent.”

It’s a system that learns how your company actually works.

What would you automate first if AI could learn by watching your best people work?

A year ago, I was using AI, but I could not really understand detailed Python code.  Today I am using Python, SQL, APIs and AI to build a decision intelligence engine. 

That feels like productivity. But how should I measure it?

For me, counting prompts, tokens or time spent using AI is not particularly useful. 

A better test is what I can now do. Can I build something I could not build before? Can I analyse more information in less time? Can I spend less time gathering data and more time thinking about the decision? How much time am I still spending checking, correcting or reworking the output?

That seems like a reasonable way to judge whether AI is making me more productive.

The enterprise question is harder, but perhaps the principle should remain simple.

Take a process before AI.

How long did it take? What did it cost? What did it produce? What was the quality?

Then compare the same process after AI.

If the same team can produce more useful work, faster, at the same or better quality, productivity has improved.

But that still does not tell us whether value has been created.

If AI saves 10,000 hours, what happened to those hours?

Did the business serve more customers? Avoid additional hiring? Reduce external spend? Improve quality? Make decisions faster? Create more revenue?

This is where measurement can easily become a rabbit hole.

Dashboards, AI KPIs, ROI models, committees and increasingly detailed frameworks can create a bureaucracy around proving that AI reduces bureaucracy.

Is this necessary? I am not convinced it is.

A central AI function can set standards, technology and governance. But the people closest to the work should be able to define what better looks like.

Finance should know whether forecasting improved. Legal should know whether contract reviews became faster without increasing risk. Technology should know whether it can deliver more reliable change with the same resources.

The measures will differ. The underlying question does not:

Are we producing more useful output from the resources we already have?

My own experiment is obviously much smaller. But I find it useful because I can see the change very clearly.

AI has taken me from asking it to explain code to helping me build something I would not have been able to build a year ago.

That is increased capability. The harder question for business is whether that capability becomes measurable productivity. And then whether that productivity becomes economic value.

Saving time creates capacity. It does not automatically create value.

I charged a founder $4,700/month for one engineer.
 
He later told me that same role, filled through a US recruiter, would have cost him $18,000/month fully loaded.
 
Same seniority. Same stack. Same output.
 
His words: "I kept waiting for the catch."
 
There was no catch. The engineer was in Karachi. Top 1% of his cohort. Eight years of production experience. AI-native workflow. First PR on day three.
 
The founder had spent four months prior trying to hire locally. Three offers declined. One who accepted and quit in week two.
 
I'm not telling this story to pitch you. I'm telling it because the mental model most founders carry into engineering hiring is completely wrong.
 
They think offshore = lower quality. They think speed = corners cut. They think month-to-month = instability.
 
Those assumptions made sense in 2015.
 
In 2026, the best engineers aren't in San Francisco. They're distributed. They use the same tools. They ship the same code. And the ones who've been building on AI-native workflows for two years run circles around engineers still learning what Cursor is.
 
Geography is not quality. Timezone is not commitment. Contract length is not trust.
 
Your hiring assumptions might be the most expensive thing on your cap table.

More applicants do not automatically make a hire easier.

Across accounting, finance, compliance, audit, risk, governance, procurement, and contracts roles, rising application volume can create a false sense of an employer’s market.

In practice, it often means more filtering: not better candidates.

Many applications are generic or heavily AI-tailored. Meanwhile, the strongest candidates are still selective about the roles they pursue and the organizations they trust.

A better approach:

1. Define what the role truly requires. Separate must-haves from preferences before reviewing resumes.

2. Keep the process moving. Delays can cost you candidates who are already evaluating other opportunities.

3. Respect the candidate experience. Clear communication and focused interviews help qualified people stay engaged.

Application volume is a resource to manage: not proof of an easy hire.

The goal is not to collect more resumes. It is to identify the right capability, judgment, and fit for the work ahead.

Five years ago, a data analyst wrote SQL and built dashboards, and a data engineer built the pipelines that fed them. The border was clear enough that job postings could just say which one they meant.

That border is mostly gone now.

Building a Power BI semantic model taught me the DAX and star-schema side. Building a local RAG pipeline taught me the ingestion, chunking, and embedding side. Neither felt like the other job while I was doing it. They felt like the same skill, applied to different endpoints.

Tools pushed this from both directions. dbt turned transformation into something analysts write. Fabric and Databricks put pipeline orchestration and BI on the same platform. Nobody hands you a laptop that only does one half anymore.

Client and hiring expectations moved faster than job titles did. Data analyst postings now list dbt and orchestration tools. Data engineer postings now expect you to explain the metric, not just move it. The title on the contract rarely matches the actual ask.

AI compresses the gap further. A model that writes a transformation query does not care whether a human would have called that analytics work or engineering work. It just writes the query. The distinction was always more organizational than technical, and AI has no reason to respect an org chart.

None of this means the roles are identical. Someone still owns uptime and someone still owns the story in the number. But the skill overlap in the middle used to be a thin strip, and now it is most of the job.

Where do you actually draw the line on your team these days, if you still draw one at all?

A commercial HVAC contractor in Dallas was spending $6,000 USD a month on Google Ads.

His objective: replacement and maintenance for 25-ton rooftop packaged units across industrial warehouses.

His account had a 94% "Optimization Score" after following Google's automated advice: switch all keywords to Broad Match to "capture relevant traffic."

When I pulled his Search Terms report, the reality was staggering:
- "How to fix a rattling fan in my GE refrigerator"
- "HVAC apprentice jobs near me hiring immediately"
- "Cheap window air conditioner repair Dallas Craigslist"
- "HVAC technician training school tuition cost"

Google's broad match AI saw "HVAC" and treated an apprentice seeking a job as equivalent to a property director looking to replace a $35,000 chiller.

Over $3,800 USD of his monthly budget was subsidizing employment searchers and DIY repairs.

We stripped out 40 broad keywords, locked in phrase match constraints for commercial terms, and uploaded 180 negative keywords.

Ad spend dropped by 50%. Qualified commercial bid requests tripled within thirty days.

Google's default algorithms do not care if a click turns into a high-margin contract. They only care about selling auction inventory.

When was the last time you reviewed your raw Search Terms report to see what Google's broad match is actually buying? Follow along for honest accounts of commercial ad spend.
